When eligibility is ambiguous, the interpretation belongs to the funder, reached through whoever manages that relationship, and it must be settled before the money is spent, because ineligible spending is recovered after the fact and recovery is far harder than prevention.
questions.mindset: Settle whose rules govern the money before deciding what the money can buy.

questions.stem: Midway through a two-year flood-warning systems project, the organisation's finance function raises the overhead rate charged on every internal labour hour from 18 to 26 per cent, backdated to the start of the financial year. The project's cost performance index falls from 1.00 to 0.94 overnight, although productivity and spending on the work itself are unchanged. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Report the variance separately as a rate change outside the project's control, showing the indices with and without it so the sponsor can see underlying performance.
options.rationale: Separating the rate effect from delivery performance stops a corporate charging decision from being read as a project failing. The sponsor sees both the true efficiency of the work and the cost the organisation has added.

options.text: Re-forecast the estimate at completion using the new overhead rate for all remaining labour, and tell the sponsor how much additional funding the change implies.
options.rationale: The new rate applies to every remaining hour, so the forecast has to carry it. Quantifying the funding gap early gives the sponsor time to decide whether to fund it or change the plan.

options.text: Start a corrective action plan to recover the 6 per cent through productivity gains in the remaining work packages, so that the project index returns to 1.00.
options.rationale: Corrective action addresses performance, and performance has not changed. Asking the team to work faster to absorb a charging decision treats a rate variance as an efficiency variance.

options.text: Draw on the contingency reserve to cover the higher overhead charges, since the increase is an unforeseen cost event that has fallen on the project's budget.
options.rationale: Contingency is held for the identified risks it was sized against. Spending it on a corporate rate change leaves those risks uncovered and hides a funding question that belongs to the sponsor.

options.text: Ask finance to exempt the project from the new rate, on the grounds that its budget was approved under the old rate and corporate charges are outside its control.
options.rationale: The rate is an organisation-wide decision and the project has no standing to opt out of it. Seeking an exemption spends effort resisting a change that should simply be reflected in the forecast and funding.

questions.explanation: A variance caused by a change in a charging rate is not a performance problem and should not be managed as one. Separate rate effects from efficiency in reporting, carry the new rate into the forecast for all remaining work, and take the resulting funding gap to whoever owns the budget. Absorbing it through reserves or productivity targets misdiagnoses where the cost came from.
questions.mindset: Accept a change you cannot control, then make sure everyone can see what it did to the numbers.

questions.stem: Consolidating estimates for a hybrid retail-systems programme, you find that each of the five workstream leads has quietly added a 15 to 20 per cent 'safety margin' to their packages. The programme also holds a contingency reserve of €400,000 sized from the risk register. Two leads say the margins protect them from being blamed for overruns. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Ask each lead to separate the margin from the base estimate and name the risks it was meant to cover, so those risks can be assessed alongside the rest of the register.
options.rationale: The margins may be protecting against real risks the register missed. Surfacing them turns private worry into named, assessable risk, and it addresses the blame concern by showing that risk is managed openly rather than absorbed by individuals.

options.text: Re-size the programme contingency from the combined risks once the hidden margins are removed, and hold it visibly at programme level with clear rules for drawing it down.
options.rationale: Pooled, visible contingency covers the same exposure with less money than five hidden buffers, because not every risk occurs at once. Clear drawdown rules give leads a legitimate route to cover when a risk does materialise.

options.text: Remove the margins from every package without further discussion and return the money to the sponsor, since the contingency reserve already covers the programme's identified risks.
options.rationale: This assumes the register already captures everything the margins were protecting against, without checking. It also confirms the leads' fear of being exposed, which is likely to drive the padding somewhere harder to find.

options.text: Leave the margins in place but cut the programme contingency by the same total, so that the overall budget stays the same and the risk cover is not counted twice.
options.rationale: It fixes the double count on paper while keeping the cover hidden and unpooled. Buffers held inside packages tend to be spent whether or not the risks occur, so the money is consumed without being controlled.

options.text: Accept the margins as each lead's professional judgement, and make clear that any overruns will be met from that workstream's own buffer before the programme reserve is touched.
options.rationale: Respecting judgement is reasonable, but this formalises the hidden buffers rather than examining them. The programme ends up double-funded for some risks and blind to which ones the money is held against.

questions.explanation: Hidden buffers double-count risk that contingency already covers, cannot be pooled across workstreams, and tend to be consumed whether or not the risk occurs. Risk allowances should be explicit, tied to named risks, and held where they can be pooled and controlled. When padding is defensive, removing the cause, a culture of blame for honest estimates, matters as much as removing the padding.
questions.mindset: Bring hidden allowances into the open, where they can be sized, pooled and controlled.

questions.stem: Your product team's quarterly funding covers its eight people and a test environment. Load testing shows that when the new route-planning feature opens to all 40,000 customers next quarter, cloud mapping and compute charges will rise from about £3,000 to £22,000 a month. The product owner says running costs belong to operations after launch, but operations has no budget line for this service. Which two actions should the delivery lead take?

options.text: Add the projected running costs to next quarter's funding request and to the product's business case, so the investment decision reflects what the feature costs to run.
options.rationale: A feature that costs £22,000 a month to run is a different investment from one that does not. Putting the cost into the funding request and business case makes it part of the decision instead of a surprise after launch.

options.text: Show the product owner which parts of the feature drive the mapping charges, so cost per use can be weighed alongside value when ordering the remaining backlog.
options.rationale: Running cost is a product attribute the product owner can manage once it is visible. Knowing which behaviours drive the charges lets backlog decisions trade cost against value rather than discovering the bill afterwards.

options.text: Ask operations to raise a budget request for the service before launch, since running costs after release fall under their remit rather than under the product team's.
options.rationale: It assumes an ownership arrangement that does not yet exist. The team holds the numbers and the knowledge of what drives them, and leaving the request to a function with no budget line risks launching with the cost unfunded.

options.text: Hold the launch to a smaller group of customers for now, so that monthly charges stay within the team's current funding until someone agrees who will pay for the full rollout.
options.rationale: Phased rollout is a valid tactic, but choosing it to stay inside a budget gap makes a product decision on financial grounds without telling the people who fund it. The gap stays hidden while value is held back.

options.text: Re-engineer the feature to use a cheaper mapping provider before launch, adding the work to the next two sprints so that running costs fall back to a level the team can absorb.
options.rationale: It commits two sprints to cost reduction before anyone has decided the cost is unacceptable for the value delivered. The trade-off belongs to the product owner and funders once they can see it.

questions.explanation: A product's financial picture includes what it costs to run, not just what it costs to build. When design choices create recurring costs, those costs belong in funding requests, business cases and backlog decisions before launch, because once a feature is live the cost is already committed and the question of who pays becomes a dispute rather than a decision.
questions.mindset: Count what it costs to run as well as what it costs to build.

questions.stem: A product company is making three spending decisions about its booking platform. Match each decision to the cost concept that should drive it. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Whether to move the only engineer who understands the payment gateway onto this team, when doing so postpones a client integration worth €30,000 in fees.
Whether to pay €15,000 for an extra fortnight of contractor capacity to finish the release, given that the team's salaries and tooling are paid either way.
Whether a €20,000 fee to expedite a third-party security audit is worth paying, given that each week of later launch forgoes about €8,000 of subscription revenue.

options.text: Opportunity cost: the value of the best alternative given up
options.rationale: Moving the engineer costs nothing on the payroll but gives up €30,000 of client fees. The value of the alternative forgone is the real cost of the move, and it is invisible in any budget line.

options.text: Incremental cost: only the costs that change because of the decision
options.rationale: Salaries and tooling are paid whichever way the decision goes, so they are irrelevant to it. Only the €15,000 of contractor cost changes, and that is what has to be weighed against finishing the release.

options.text: Cost of delay: the value lost for each unit of time the outcome arrives later
options.rationale: At about €8,000 a week of forgone revenue, the expedite fee pays for itself if it brings launch forward by roughly two and a half weeks or more. Expressing time as money is what makes the fee comparable.

options.text: Sunk cost: money already spent that cannot be recovered
options.rationale: Not used. Sunk cost matters in decisions only as something to ignore, and none of these three turns on money already spent. Each is about future costs and value that still depend on the choice made.

questions.explanation: A spending decision should be driven by the costs and value that actually change with it. That means counting what is given up as well as what is paid, ignoring costs incurred either way, and pricing time when the benefit depends on when the outcome arrives. Choosing the right cost concept first stops irrelevant figures, often the largest ones on the page, from deciding the question.
questions.mindset: Count only what the decision changes, including what it gives up and what it delays.

questions.stem: Reviewing estimates across a hybrid transport infrastructure programme, the project management office finds three different problems. Match each to the corrective technique that addresses its cause. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Before estimating a bridge refurbishment, the engineers were told the board 'expects around £2m', and all three supposedly independent estimates came in between £1.9m and £2.1m.
Every package in a signalling upgrade was estimated assuming nothing goes wrong, and the organisation's last eight signalling projects finished on average 34 per cent over their estimates.
A business unit submitted a low estimate for its own scheme, and later emails show its team knew the figure was unrealistic but feared the scheme would otherwise lose the funding round.

options.text: Produce estimates before any target or expected figure is shared with the estimators
options.rationale: Three estimates clustering around a figure the board mentioned is the signature of anchoring. The fix is to remove the anchor from the process, since estimators cannot reliably ignore a number once they have heard it.

options.text: Adjust the estimate using actual outturns from a reference class of comparable past projects
options.rationale: Bottom-up estimates built on a no-problems view miss the overrun that comparable projects consistently show. Reference class forecasting brings in the outside view, here a 34 per cent history, which inside-view estimating cannot see.

options.text: Have an independent cost review that reports to the investment board, not to the sponsoring unit
options.rationale: When the estimators have a reason to understate, better technique does not help because the error is deliberate. An independent review accountable to the funder removes the incentive from the people producing the figure.

options.text: Apply a flat 10 per cent uplift to every estimate in the programme
options.rationale: Not used. A uniform uplift treats three different causes as one error of size and corrects none of them. It is too small for the signalling history, arbitrary for the bridge, and leaves the incentive behind the third estimate untouched.

questions.explanation: Estimating errors have causes, and the correction has to match the cause: anchoring is fixed by removing the anchor before estimating, optimism by bringing in outturn data from comparable projects, and deliberate understatement by moving review away from those with a reason to understate. A blanket uplift treats symptoms and leaves every one of those causes in place for the next estimate.
questions.mindset: Diagnose why an estimate is wrong before deciding how to correct it.

questions.stem: Your cost management plan lets each work package choose how its earned value is credited. Complete each sentence with the method that fits the work. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: A two-day independent safety inspection that starts and finishes inside a single monthly reporting period should earn value using
A nine-month tunnelling package with six physically verifiable milestones, each agreed with the client's engineer, should earn value using
Project controls support that runs for the whole project and produces no discrete deliverable of its own should earn value using

options.text: the 0/100 rule, crediting value only when the work is complete
options.rationale: Work that starts and finishes within one reporting period never needs partial credit. Crediting it only on completion is simple and cannot overstate progress.

options.text: weighted milestones, crediting an agreed share as each milestone is verified
options.rationale: A long package needs progress credited along the way, and verifiable milestones agreed with the client give objective points to credit it at, rather than someone's estimate of percentage complete.

options.text: level of effort, crediting value in step with the passage of time
options.rationale: Support work has no product to measure, so its value is earned as time passes. It should be kept small and separate, because it always shows on schedule and can mask variances in discrete work.

options.text: the 50/50 rule, crediting half at the start and half at completion
options.rationale: Not used. The 50/50 rule suits short work that spans two reporting periods. The inspection fits within one, the tunnelling is far too long, and the support work has no point of completion to credit.

questions.explanation: The earned value method should match how progress on the work can be objectively observed. Short work inside one period needs no partial credit, long work needs objective intermediate points, and support work with no product is earned by time and kept apart from discrete work. Choosing a method that lets someone estimate progress where it could be measured invites earned value to drift ahead of reality.
questions.mindset: Credit progress the way it can be verified, not the way it can be estimated.

questions.stem: A theatre's air-handling upgrade has three work packages with three-point cost estimates (optimistic / most likely / pessimistic, in £ thousands): sensors 40 / 50 / 72; chillers 180 / 210 / 300; controls software 60 / 75 / 120. Using beta (PERT) weighting and treating the packages as independent, work out the expected cost of the whole upgrade, its standard deviation, and how far the expected cost sits above the sum of the most likely figures.

blanks.label: Expected cost of the whole upgrade, in £ thousands
blanks.rationale: Each package's expected cost is (O + 4M + P) ÷ 6: sensors (40 + 200 + 72) ÷ 6 = 52, chillers (180 + 840 + 300) ÷ 6 = 220, software (60 + 300 + 120) ÷ 6 = 80. The total is 52 + 220 + 80 = 352.

blanks.label: Standard deviation of the total, in £ thousands, to one decimal place
blanks.rationale: Each package's standard deviation is (P − O) ÷ 6: 5.33, 20 and 10. Standard deviations do not add; variances do: 28.4 + 400 + 100 = 528.4, and its square root is about 23.0.

blanks.label: Amount by which the expected cost exceeds the sum of the most likely figures, in £ thousands
blanks.rationale: The most likely figures sum to 50 + 210 + 75 = 335. Every package is skewed towards overrun, so the expected cost of 352 sits 17 above it, which is what a single-point estimate built from most likely values leaves out.

questions.explanation: Three-point estimating gives an expected value and a measure of spread for each package. Expected values add directly, but spread combines through variances, so the total's standard deviation is the square root of the summed variances, not the sum of the standard deviations. When estimates are skewed towards overrun, a budget built from most likely figures is systematically low, and the gap is a cost to plan for rather than a risk to hope away.
questions.mindset: Treat the most likely figure as a point on a range, not as the estimate.

questions.stem: A Monte Carlo simulation of a ferry terminal refurbishment's total cost, against a base estimate of £4.6m, produced the five points shown. Company policy sets the budget at the lowest figure that gives at least 80 per cent confidence of not being exceeded, with contingency covering the gap above the base estimate. Select the figure the budget should be set at.

graphic.title: Five simulated total-cost outcomes with the probability that each will be exceeded
graphic.caption: Select a cost figure. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between them, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: £4.6m (base estimate): 70% chance of being exceeded
regions.rationale: The base estimate has only a 30 per cent chance of holding. Budgeting at it means no contingency at all and an overrun in seven simulated outcomes out of ten.

regions.label: £4.9m: 45% chance of being exceeded
regions.rationale: This is close to the median outcome, giving about 55 per cent confidence. It is a common choice because it feels like a realistic central figure, but it falls well short of the 80 per cent the policy requires.

regions.label: £5.2m: 25% chance of being exceeded
regions.rationale: A 25 per cent chance of being exceeded means 75 per cent confidence, just below the threshold. Reading the exceedance figure as if it were the confidence level is the slip that leads here.

regions.label: £5.4m: 15% chance of being exceeded
regions.rationale: A 15 per cent chance of being exceeded is 85 per cent confidence of not being exceeded, and this is the lowest figure that meets the 80 per cent policy. Contingency is £5.4m − £4.6m = £0.8m.

regions.label: £5.8m: 5% chance of being exceeded
regions.rationale: This meets the policy comfortably, but the policy asks for the lowest figure that does. Budgeting here ties up £0.4m more than the organisation decided it needed to hold.

questions.explanation: A simulation turns a single estimate into a range of outcomes, and a confidence policy picks a point on that range. Confidence of not exceeding a figure is one minus the chance of exceeding it, and the budget is the lowest figure that meets the required confidence: anything lower under-reserves and anything higher locks up money the organisation chose not to hold. The contingency is then the distance from the base estimate to that point.
questions.mindset: Convert the probability to the form the policy uses before reading the chart.
